title: Architecture & Standards: API, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs
author: Samira Chen
content:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards: API design, coding conventions, infrastructure and IaC guidelines, model-serving requirements, observability/telemetry conventions, performance SLOs, and the Decision Record (ADR) process. It is intended as the canonical reference for architects, service owners, and platform engineers.

Goals
- Ensure predictable, maintainable, and secure service APIs and infrastructure.
- Reduce cognitive load across teams via standard conventions.
- Enable reliable model serving with predictable latency and cost.
- Make telemetry actionable and consistent across the stack.
- Provide a lightweight but auditable ADR process for cross-team decisions.

1) API Standards

Overview
All public and internal HTTP APIs follow a single, documented standard to keep client and server codebases simple and interoperable. Where gRPC provides measurable advantages for internal high-throughput paths, use ADRs (see section 8) to approve.

Key rules
- Versioning: Use semantic versioning at the API surface (e.g., /v1/models, /v2/embeddings). Backwards-incompatible changes require a major version bump and an ADR describing migration paths.
- Resource-oriented design: Prefer plural nouns for resource paths (e.g., POST /v1/models, GET /v1/models/{model_id}/versions).
- HTTP verbs and status codes: Use 2xx for success, 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors. Return specific codes: 400 (validation), 401 (auth), 403 (permission), 404 (not found), 429 (rate limit), 503 (unavailable).
- Error format: All errors must return JSON with keys: code, message, request_id, details (optional). Example: {"code":"model_not_found","message":"Model not found","request_id":"..."}.
- Idempotency: For non-idempotent endpoints (e.g., job creation), accept Idempotency-Key header and persist server-side keys for at least 24 hours.
- Pagination: Use cursor-based pagination with `next_cursor` and `limit` parameters for large lists. Avoid page/offset for model catalogs.
- Rate limiting and headers: Implement per-API and per-key rate limits. Expose `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers. 429 responses must include `Retry-After`.
- OpenAPI: Maintain an accurate OpenAPI 3.1 spec in the repo `api/openapi.yaml`. The spec is a source of truth used by SDK generation pipelines.
- Authentication: Use bearer tokens (JWT for internal service tokens, opaque tokens for customer API keys). All endpoints require TLS (mTLS for internal control-plane endpoints).

API Lifecycle
- Design: Create an API design doc and OpenAPI draft.
- Review: API review with API guild and platform team.
- Implement: Auto-generate server/client stubs where appropriate.
- Deprecation: Announce deprecations at least 90 days before removal and provide migration docs.

2) Coding Standards and CI Quality Gates

Languages and style
- Python: follow PEP8 with black (line-length 88) and isort. Type annotations required for public modules.
- Go: follow gofmt; use staticcheck and go vet.
- Rust/C++: apply team-specific style guides; include Clippy or clang-tidy.

Quality gates (required in PR pipeline)
- Linting pass (language-specific).
- Unit and integration tests with >= 80% coverage for critical path code; service-level tests as applicable.
- Static type checks (mypy for Python).
- Security scan: dependency scanning (Snyk/OSS), secret scanning.
- IaC drift checks for Terraform changes.

Branching and releases
- Trunk-based development for production services. Feature branches must be short-lived and merged via PR.
- Releases: semantic versioning for libraries and artifacts. Service images tagged with git SHA and semver.

3) Infrastructure & IaC Standards

Terraform and modules
- Structure: Central `terraform-modules` repo for shared modules (vpc, eks/gke, gpu-pool, kms, logging). Module versions are pinned and published to our private module registry.
- Naming: Use standardized resource names: r-{team}-{env}-{service}-{resource}. Example: r-infra-prod-redwood-serving-natgw-01.
- State management: Remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locks (or cloud equivalent) and MFA protected admin flows.

Security & networking
- Network segregation: prod, staging, dev VPCs. Control planes on a separate VPC with strict peering.
- KMS & secrets: Integrate with cloud KMS/HSM and HashiCorp Vault for short-lived credentials. Secrets must never be in plaintext in repo.
- RBAC: Least privilege for IAM roles and service accounts; periodic access reviews every 90 days.

Observability for infra changes
- Every module should emit relevant Terraform plan metadata to an audit log and CI job that creates a change ticket.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Deployment and versioning
- Model artifacts: Store models in an immutable artifact registry with metadata (model_id, architecture, tokenizer_version, quantization_profile, commit_sha).
- Pinning: Serving configs must pin model artifact identifiers (no floating tags in production).
- Canary/rollout: Support canary traffic split at the request router with rollback triggers on quality or latency regressions.

Serving runtime configuration
- Batching: Configure per-model batching targets. Defaults: batch_size_target = 32 for GPU-backed models; tailorable per-model via profiling.
- KV cache policy: Cache prefix KV for chat sessions with configurable TTL; sensitive prompts must not be cached.
- Fallbacks: Define compatible fallback model families for graceful degradation (e.g., 8-bit quantized variant).
- Quantization profiles: Maintain `quantization-profiles` directory with vetted profiles and supported hardware matrix.

Testing & quality
- Evaluation harness: Every model push must run deterministic evals against the team's acceptance prompt-set and report regressions.
- Performance baseline: Capture throughput/latency profiled under representative workloads and store as artifact.

5) Observability Standards

Metrics (Prometheus style)
- Naming convention: <service>_<resource>_<metric>_<unit>; use snake_case. Examples: serving_inference_requests_total (counter), serving_request_latency_seconds (histogram).
- Labels: include service, model_id, model_version, region, route, env. Avoid high-cardinality labels (user_id only in traces or sampled logs).

Tracing
- Use OpenTelemetry (OTEL) for traces. Enforce trace context propagation across service boundaries. Typical spans: request.receive -> router.dispatch -> runtime.kv_cache -> runtime.infer -> storage.write.
- Sampling: 100% sampling for error traces; 1-5% for success traces by default with tail-based sampling on anomalies.

Logging
- JSON structured logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, trace_id, message, fields. Example: {"timestamp":...,"level":"info","service":"serving","request_id":"..."}.

Dashboards and alerts
- Dashboards: Per-service overview (latency, error rate, throughput, cost per token), plus model-specific dashboards imported from `dashboards/model_serving` templates.
- Alerting: Define alerts mapped to runbooks. Examples: SLO burn rate > 2x for 15m, p99 latency breach, 5xx error rate > 1% sustained for 10m. All alerts must page oncall and create an incident ticket.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

Service tiers and SLOs (examples)
- Hosted API (public free/prod): Availability SLO 99.9% monthly. p95 latency target for generation endpoints: <= 500ms (short prompts), p99 latency target <= 2s.
- Dedicated (reserved): Availability SLO 99.95%. p95 latency target depends on contract; baseline: <= 350ms.
- Private (on-prem): Availability SLOs are contractual; recommend targets documented in deployment runbook.

Model-serving performance targets
- GPU inference throughput baselines: Provide per-HW baseline table in profiling docs (example values):
  - A100 80GB: 120 tokens/sec for Llama-2-13B FP16 (batch 32)
  - H100: 220 tokens/sec for same model
- Tail latency: For synchronous generate APIs, p99 should be within 3x of p95 for production traffic; investigate large p99 skews.

Cost controls
- Token cost budget alerts: track cost-per-token by model and route; alert when 7-day rolling cost exceeds budget threshold.
- Autoscaling rules should prefer latency headroom for critical routes and cost savings for background jobs.

7) Security and Compliance Touchpoints

- Data residency: Tag datasets and customer tenants with residency requirements; routing must honor region constraints.
- Audit logs: All control-plane operations (model uploads, keys, infra changes) must be auditable.
- Secrets rotation: Keys must rotate at least annually or on suspicion of exposure.

8) ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) Process

Purpose
Use ADRs to record cross-cutting architectural decisions that have long-term implications (API contracts, infra primitives, major runtime choices). ADRs create an audit trail and facilitate knowledge transfer.

ADR template (must be used verbatim)
- ADR-ID: ADR-YYYY-NNN (e.g., ADR-2025-012)
- Title: short title
- Status: proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD
- Authors: list
- Context: short background
- Decision: summary of decision
- Consequences: operational, technical, and migration impacts
- Related ADRs/pages: list

ADR workflow
1. Draft ADR in `architecture/adrs/` repo and create PR.
2. Notify architecture guild and affected teams; reviewers provide feedback within 7 business days.
3. Merge when at least two approvers (one from platform/infra and one from runtime/product) accept.
4. Mark status accepted and publish to Confluence; link to implementation tickets.

Example ADR summary
- ADR-ID: ADR-2025-007
- Title: Use REST for external APIs; gRPC for internal high-throughput paths
- Status: accepted (2025-05-12)
- Decision: Public customer-facing endpoints remain REST/HTTP+JSON for interoperability. Internal model-to-runtime communication and heavy data-plane flows may use gRPC for performance and streaming support. Implement instrumentation requirements for gRPC paths to match HTTP observability.
- Consequences: Dual stack maintained for a period; extra SDK support for internal clients; ADR outlines migration checklist.

9) Ownership and Governance

- Architecture guild: Quarterly reviews of standards and ADR backlog. Members include reps from serving runtime, infra, platform, security, and product.
- Service owners: Maintain API spec, telemetry, and runbooks. Owners must respond to alerts within SLA and keep docs current.
- Standards review: Major revisions require a published changelog and a 30-day comment period before moving to `published`.

10) Related artifacts and runbooks
- `api/openapi.yaml` (source of truth for public APIs)
- `quantization-profiles/` (model-serving profiles)
- `dashboards/` templates and `runbooks/` per-alert playbooks
- `architecture/adrs/` repo with ADR markdown files
- `infra/terraform-modules/` internal module registry

Appendix: Quick-check checklist for new service
1. API OpenAPI draft created and reviewed.
2. Linting and CI gates configured.
3. Terraform module or minimal infra reviewed.
4. Telemetry metrics and dashboards scaffolded.
5. SLOs defined and alerting connected to runbook.
6. ADR created for any cross-cutting architectural decision.
